rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God withdraws blessings only when people's inner selves become depraved.
rows.anchor: God does not withdraw His blessings from men unless their inner selves become depraved

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God also withholds blessings from wilful sinners until they reform their inner disposition and become worthy of grace.
rows.anchor: does not bestow His blessings upon wilful sinners until they change their inner disposition and become worthy of His grace

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: More broadly, the verse illustrates God's law of cause and effect: civilizations rise or fall with people's moral qualities and inner changes.
rows.anchor: illustration of the divine law of cause and effect (sunnat Allah) which dominates the lives of both individuals and communities

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators take kadhalika to mean that Muhammad was sent as earlier prophets had been sent.
rows.anchor: Most of the commentators explain the "thus" or "thus it is" (kadhalika) as referring to the earlier prophets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad rejects the speculative interpolation that the phrase refers to earlier prophets as unnecessary.
rows.anchor: this speculative interpolation is unnecessary

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He links "thus" to God's guidance of those who turn to Him, making Muhammad's mission an instrument of divine guidance.
rows.anchor: the adverb "thus" connects directly with the preceding statement that God "guides unto Himself all who turn unto Him"

rows.speaker: Tabari
rows.claim: Asad says Tabari apparently understands the phrase in the same way he does.
rows.anchor: apparently, how Tabari understands the above phrase

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari and Razi
rows.claim: They read the passing communities as an indirect reference to prophetic revelation continuing through Muhammad, the Last Prophet.
rows.anchor: an indirect reference to the continuity of prophetic revelation before and up to the time of the Last Prophet, Muhammad (Zamakhshari, Razi)

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathir
rows.claim: The added words "of unbelievers" in Asad's rendering draw on Ibn Kathir's commentary.
rows.anchor: The interpolation of the words "of unbelievers" is based on Ibn Kathir's commentary on this verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders arsalnaka as "raised thee as Our Apostle" because English requires it before the following preposition "amidst".
rows.anchor: my rendering of arsalnaka (lit., "We have sent thee") as "We have raised thee as Our Apostle" is necessitated, in English, by the subsequent preposition "amidst"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial of the Most Gracious may mean denying God's existence, rejecting His guidance, or associating divine qualities with other beings or forces.
rows.anchor: by refusing to acknowledge His existence, or by rejecting His guidance, or by ascribing divine qualities to other beings or forces side by side with Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ancient Arabian usage, "days" could denote momentous historical events; ayyam al-'arab named the pre-Islamic intertribal wars metonymically.
rows.anchor: the terms "day" or "days" were often used to describe momentous historical events (e.g., ayyam al-'arab as a metonym for the inter-tribal wars of pre-Islamic Arabia)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Qur'anic "day" language commonly concerns eschatology, and 45:14 clearly points to final judgment, Asad reads God's Days here as the Resurrection judgment.
rows.anchor: and, particularly, in view of 45:14, where the expression "the Days of God" unmistakably points to His judgment at the end of time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural may stress that the Qur'anic Day is an ultimate reality beyond human definitions of time, where time has no meaning.
rows.anchor: the plural form ("the Days of God") is perhaps meant to bring out the idea that the "Day" of which the Qur'an so often speaks has nothing to do with human time-definitions

rows.speaker: Suyuti
rows.claim: Suyuti dates the surah to shortly after surah 12, in the last year before the Prophet's migration to Medina.
rows.anchor: According to Suyuti, this sura h was revealed very shortly after surah 12 (Yasuf)

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi proposes that verse 87 was revealed at Medina.
rows.anchor: supposition (mentioned by Razi) that verse 87 was revealed at Medina

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad dismisses the proposed Medinan dating of verse 87 because it has no factual corroboration.
rows.anchor: lacks any factual corroboration and may, therefore, be safely dismissed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah's main theme is God's creative activity and guidance through revelation, especially the Qur'an, which verse 9 predicts will remain incorruptible.
rows.anchor: the Qur'an, which, as verse 9 pred icts, will for all times remain impervious to corruption

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title Al-Hijr comes from the named Arabian region in verse 80; the Companions likely chose it because of old legends attached to the place.
rows.anchor: obviously 'suggested itself to the Prophet's Companions because of the many legends attached to that place-name since 'time immemorial.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad treats Al-Hijr as a historical place name rather than a description, citing ancient references to Hegra or Egra, and therefore leaves it untranslated.
rows.anchor: a place-name and not a description ("rocky tract" or according to some, "forbidden tract") is evident from the fact

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sincere servants are deeply conscious of God, so Satan's blandishments cannot lead them astray.
rows.anchor: those who are so deeply conscious of God that no "blandishment of Satan" can lead them astray

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan has no power over people except those who voluntarily follow him from among the lost.
rows.anchor: except him who shall follow thee from among those who are lost in grievous error

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As 14:22 says, Satan only called and his followers responded; this passage therefore differs essentially from 7:11-18.
rows.anchor: I had no power at all over you: I but called you - and you responded unto me

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to his note 114 on surah 11 for this verse's explanation.
rows.anchor: See surah 11, note 114

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari and Razi
rows.claim: Mutawassim denotes someone who studies a thing's outward appearance to understand its real nature and inner characteristics.
rows.anchor: one who applies his mind to the study of the outward appearance of a thing with a view to understanding its real nature and its inner characteristics

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's showing the path's goal means establishing the ethical and moral aims implied by the right path.
rows.anchor: the establishing of the goals of ethics and morality implied in the concept of the "right path"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase that the duty rests on God parallels His self-imposed law of grace and mercy; He shows the right path to everyone willing to follow it.
rows.anchor: the expression "it rests upon God" ('ala 'llah) is similar in intent to the statement in 6:12 and 54 that He "has willed upon Himself the law of grace and mercy"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because moral choice between good and evil is God-given, God does not impose guidance but leaves people free to accept or reject it.
rows.anchor: God does not "impose" His guidance upon man but leaves it to him to accept or reject it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage closes the account of God's favors by returning to man's intellectual potential, his greatest gift, linked with verses 4, 8, and 14 and the creation allegory in 2:30-33.
rows.anchor: the theme introduced in verse 4 and alluded to, indirectly, in the last sentence of verse 8 as well as in verse 14:namely, the consideration of man's intellectual potential - the greatest of all the gifts bestowed upon him by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awha highlights bee instinct: it builds an exceptionally ordered, economical honeycomb from proportioned hexagonal prismatic wax cells.
rows.anchor: the wonderful quality of the instinct which enables the lowly insect to construct the geometrical masterpiece of a honeycomb out of perfectly-proportioned hexagonal, prismatic wax cells

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bee's honey-making transformation, together with its instinctive building, demonstrates God's ways throughout nature.
rows.anchor: Together with the subsequently mentioned transmutation, in the bee's body, of plant juices into honey, this provides a striking evidence of "God's ways" manifested in all nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad notes that the phrase literally means "thy Sustainer's paths".
rows.anchor: Lit., "thy Sustainer's paths"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders the metaphorical al-'arsh as "the throne of His almightiness", referring to his explanation at 7:54, note 43.
rows.anchor: For my rendering of the metaphorical term al-'arsh as "the throne of His almightiness"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad refers readers to surah 7, note 145, for his rendering of al-asma' al-husna.
rows.anchor: For an explanation of this rendering of al-asma' al-husna, see surah 7, note 145

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Arabic uses the past tense, the sentence describes creation as continuous and timeless, an unceasing present.
rows.anchor: it is independent of the concept of time and denotes, as in so many other places in the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalq here includes both a thing's inner nature and the outward form in which that nature appears, explaining Asad's composite translation.
rows.anchor: The term khalq signifies in this context not merely the inner nature of a created thing or being but also the outward form in which this nature manifests itself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad traces the underlying idea to 87:2-3, among the earliest Qur'anic revelations.
rows.anchor: The idea underlying the above sentence is expressed for the first time in 87:2-3

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad supplies Pharaoh's implied question: were earlier generations who worshipped multiple gods irretrievably doomed?
rows.anchor: who used to worship a plurality of deities: are they, in thy view, irretrievably doomed?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone decrees earlier generations' afterlife destiny because He knows their motives and errors and can assess their spiritual merits and demerits.
rows.anchor: He alone knows their motives and understands the cause of their errors

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi takes the dialogue to end temporarily at this point and verses 53-55 as direct discourse to humanity.
rows.anchor: According to Razi, the dialogue between Moses and Pharaoh ends here for the time being, with verses 53-55 representing a direct Qur'anic discourse addressed to man in general

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earth's ways and means include material and intellectual resources for earning a livelihood on and from the earth.
rows.anchor: has provided you with ways and means - both material and intellectual - to gain your livelihood on earth and from it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Azwaj literally means "pairs" but apparently means "kinds" here; Asad points to 13:3, note 7.
rows.anchor: a term which in this context apparently denotes "kinds"; but see also 13:3 and the corresponding note 7

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to note 38 on 19:52 and to 2:63 and 2:83 for the covenant with the Israelites.
rows.anchor: As regards God's "covenant" with the children of Israel, see 2:63 and 83

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an also mentions manna and quails in 2:57 and 7:160.
rows.anchor: found in the Qur'an in two other places as well (namely, in 2:57 and 7:160)

rows.speaker: Arab philologists
rows.claim: Mann can mean both the desert plants' sweet resin and anything graciously bestowed without effort by its recipient.
rows.anchor: the term mann denotes not only the sweet, resinous substance exuded by certain plants of the desert, but also everything that is "bestowed as a favour"

rows.speaker: Qamus
rows.claim: Salwa means both quail and whatever comforts people after deprivation.
rows.anchor: the term salwa signifies not merely "a quail" or "quails", but also "all that makes man content and happy after privation" (Qamus)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Together, manna and quails metonymically represent sustenance God freely provided to Moses' followers.
rows.anchor: the combination of these two terms denotes, metonymically, the gift of sustenance freely bestowed by God upon the followers of Moses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command may also mean not to act arrogantly by attributing God's favors to one's own excellence through descent from Abraham.
rows.anchor: do not attribute these favours to your own supposed excellence on account of your descent from Abraham

rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: Classical commentators almost unanimously read God's wrath as the unavoidable retribution people bring on themselves by deliberately rejecting guidance and transgressing justice.
rows.anchor: almost complete unanimity among the classical commentators in that God's "condemnation" (ghadab, lit., "wrath") is a metonym for the inescapable retribution
